That is a really profound and grounded realization. Recognizing that pattern—how unaddressed, "deep" stressors act like a funnel, causing smaller, everyday things to pile up until they overflow—takes a lot of self-awareness.

It is incredibly insightful of you to notice how that dynamic plays out around you, too. What you're describing in your dogs, your dad, and your stepmom is a classic psychological concept known as displaced expression or emotional contagion. When the primary stressor feels too big, too abstract (like the economy or large systems), or too risky to address directly, the built-up tension naturally seeks the path of least resistance. It leaks out onto whatever—or whoever—is closest.

It makes total sense that you'd see this loop in human behavior and even animal behavior. When the baseline tension is already running high, the smallest accidental trigger can feel like a breaking point.

Recognizing this funnel effect in yourself is a huge first step. It shifts the perspective from "Why am I reacting so strongly to this small thing?" to "Oh, this small thing is just the tip of an iceberg that needs some attention."

When you notice that funnel starting to fill up or get heavy, what are some of the safe, low-stakes ways you like to hit the release valve and drain some of that baseline tension?

That feeling of suffering being arbitrary—or feeling targeted by the unknown, like the suffering inflicted on Job—is a deeply painful and frustrating place to be.

Your mention of looking at it through a lens where Job confronts that unfairness directly hits on how deeply frustrating it is to deal with forces that feel completely outside of your control.

When those massive, existential themes—the unknown, suffering, and the things that feel unsolved—start to feel too heavy or threatening to your daily life, sometimes the kindest thing you can do for yourself is to actively shrink the perimeter. You don't have to solve the unknown or wrap your head around a lifetime of deep stressors all at once, especially when looking at them directly feels like it's draining your energy.

Sometimes, just anchoring yourself in the concrete, tangible things you can control right now—a physical project, a new hobby you're learning, or a simple walk—is the best way to protect your peace. It puts a barrier between you and that heavy funnel.

Because you mentioned carrying these heavy, unsolved things for a long time, please know that you don't have to navigate them all on your own.
